title: Waves, interference and boundaries
summary: The linear chain of 32 unit masses on unit springs -- the alpha = 0 case of the FPUT model. Standing waves, two pulses crossing, and reflection off a fixed versus a free end, each checked against an independent Python reference.
question: Two identical pulses travel toward each other along the chain. When they overlap, is the displacement at the crossing point doubled, cancelled, or something else -- and what comes back from a fixed end versus a free end?
prediction_prompt: Predict before you touch a control:

prediction_options.label: Two pulses meeting always doubles the displacement, whatever their relative phase.
prediction_options.feedback: Set the phase control to pi (antiphase) and watch the crossing: the displacement at the midpoint drops to zero instead. Superposition adds signed displacements, not magnitudes.

prediction_options.label: The relative phase decides the outcome: in phase adds to twice the amplitude, antiphase cancels to zero, and values in between interpolate.
prediction_options.feedback: This is what the validation table shows: phase = 0 gives a measured maximum of 2x the single-pulse amplitude and phase = pi gives 0, because this chain is exactly linear and the two pulses simply add pointwise at every instant.

prediction_options.label: A reflected pulse always comes back the same way round, regardless of what is at the end of the chain.
prediction_options.feedback: Switch the boundary control between fixed and free and single-step a pulse into the wall: a fixed end sends the pulse back inverted (negative of its incoming sign) while a free end sends it back upright.

model.summary: A chain of N unit masses connected by N unit springs, with x_0 always held at 0 (a fixed left wall) and the right end either fixed (x_N = 0) or free (x_N = x_{N-1}, zero slope). This is exactly the alpha = 0 (linear) case of the FPUT chain reproduced in experiments/physics/fput-recurrence-reproduction/, so the same normal-mode formulas apply unchanged.
model.units: Dimensionless: unit mass, unit spring constant, so time is in units of sqrt(m/k). Integrated with Stormer-Verlet at a fixed step dt = 0.1; the stability bound is dt < 2/omega_max = 1, so this step is a factor of 10 inside it.

equations.name: Right wall, free
equations.note: boundary = free (zero slope, the last spring carries no extension)

equations.name: Normal-mode frequency
equations.note: fixed-fixed chain, k = 1..N−1; this is the reproduction's dispersion relation

equations.name: Mode amplitude
equations.note: unnormalised sine-transform sum, the reproduction's mode_amplitudes formula

equations.name: Mode energy
equations.note: kinetic plus potential energy stored in mode k

equations.name: Standing-wave period
equations.note: exact for the continuous-time ODE with fixed ends

assumptions: Linear springs only (alpha = 0): the restoring force is exactly proportional to extension, so the system is linear and superposition is exact.
Unit masses and unit spring constants throughout; N = 32 masses fixed for this chapter.
A discrete chain, not a continuum string: ω_k = 2 sin(πk/2N) is not proportional to k, so short-wavelength (large k) waves are dispersive even though this model has no damping.
No damping and no driving: once launched, a wave keeps its total energy exactly (to Stormer-Verlet's roundoff).
The left end is always fixed; only the right end's boundary condition is a control.

controls.label: standing-wave mode number k
controls.description: Selects the standing-wave initial condition x_i(0) = sin(iπk/N). Only meaningful with the standing-wave presets; moving this control switches the chain into the standing-wave scenario.

controls.label: relative phase of the two pulses
controls.description: Sets the second pulse's amplitude to cos(phase) times the first: 0 is in phase (the crossing doubles), π is antiphase (the crossing cancels). Moving this control switches the chain into the two-pulse scenario.

controls.label: right boundary condition
controls.description: The left end (x_0) is always fixed; this sets the right end. A reflection off a fixed end inverts sign, off a free end it does not.

controls.label: pulse width σ
controls.description: Gaussian width of a launched pulse. A narrower pulse carries more short-wavelength content and disperses (spreads and slows) more visibly as it travels.

presets.label: Standing wave k = 1
presets.note: The fundamental: the whole chain oscillates as one arch, period T_1 = 2π/ω_1 ≈ 64.0.

presets.label: Standing wave k = 2
presets.note: One node at the midpoint; period T_2 ≈ 32.1.

presets.label: Two pulses in phase
presets.note: phase = 0: the crossing displacement doubles the single-pulse amplitude.

presets.label: Two pulses in antiphase
presets.note: phase = π: the crossing displacement cancels to zero, then the pulses re-emerge unchanged.

presets.label: Single pulse, reflecting at a fixed end
presets.note: Watch the sign flip on the way back from the right wall.

presets.label: Single pulse, reflecting at a free end
presets.note: Same pulse, free right end: it returns upright.

explanation_title: What changes, and where this stops applying

explanation.heading: Superposition is exact because the chain is linear
body: Every acceleration here is a linear function of the positions (ẍ_i = x_{i+1} + x_{i−1} − 2x_i has no x² or higher term), so if x(t) and y(t) are both solutions, x(t) + y(t) is too. That is the whole reason two pulses can be predicted by simply adding their individual profiles, and the validation table checks exactly that: the two-pulse run's crossing maximum agrees with the sum of the two single-pulse runs to floating-point roundoff, not just approximately.

The FPUT reproduction (knowledgebase/studies/physics/fput-recurrence-reproduction.md) runs the same chain with a small cubic term added (alpha = 1/4). That term makes the acceleration a nonlinear function of position, superposition stops being exact, and the modes exchange energy instead of evolving independently -- which is the recurrence that study investigates. Nothing in that mixing is visible here, by construction: alpha = 0 is exactly the regime where it cannot happen.

explanation.heading: Discreteness: the chain is not a continuous string
body: A continuous string has ω = ck: every wavelength travels at the same speed. This chain's dispersion relation ω_k = 2 sin(πk/2N) only looks like that for small k (long wavelengths, where sin(πk/2N) ≈ πk/2N); for k approaching N it flattens out, and a narrow pulse -- built from many k's -- spreads out and slows down as it travels, because its component wavelengths no longer move together. Widen the pulse-width control to reduce this effect, or narrow it to see it more clearly.

explanation.heading: No damping, one boundary condition at a time
body: Energy is conserved exactly (to Stormer-Verlet roundoff): nothing here loses amplitude on reflection or over time other than the dispersive spreading above. The left end is always fixed; only the right end's condition is a control, so a chain with two free ends is outside what this page can show.

validation_cases.description: The predefined validation points. reference.py computes the analytic dispersion relation and standing-wave periods for k = 1..8 (fixed ends), the two-pulse superposition maximum at phase 0 and pi, and the reflection sign at a fixed versus a free end, then re-runs the identical Stormer-Verlet numerics and writes validation.json. The browser re-runs the same cases in this page through waves.js and the table reports the difference.

tolerance.rationale: waves.js and reference.py run the same Stormer-Verlet algorithm in the same operation order in float64, so the two implementations agree to floating-point roundoff (observed worst relative difference on this revision: about 1e-15). This 1e-9 tolerance is the chapter's kill condition for the browser-vs-reference check. It is separate from the physics tolerance: each dispersion case also declares its own period_tolerance_relative = 0.01 for the measured period against the closed-form dispersion relation, because Stormer-Verlet carries an O(dt^2) discretisation error that the analytic formula does not.

limits: Linearity is exact only at alpha = 0. The FPUT reproduction (knowledgebase/studies/physics/fput-recurrence-reproduction.md) shows that a small cubic term (alpha = 1/4) is enough to break superposition and drive energy between modes; nothing here generalises to that case.

Discreteness: ω_k = 2 sin(πk/2N) is not proportional to k, so short-wavelength packets disperse. The continuum-string approximation used to launch a pulse (v(i,0) ∝ ∓f'(i−i0), assuming every wavelength travels at speed 1) is only accurate for pulses much wider than one lattice spacing; a narrow pulseWidth visibly disperses even before it reaches a wall.
No damping: every run conserves energy exactly except for Stormer-Verlet's O(dt^2) truncation error, so nothing here shows how a real, lossy string settles.
One boundary at a time: the left end is always fixed. Two free ends, or a boundary that itself moves or absorbs, are outside this model.
N = 32 and dt = 0.1 are fixed for this chapter (not controls); the validation grid and the convergence entry hold N fixed and only vary dt to show the O(dt^2) scaling.
